article.title: Goodbye Claude, Hello Pi
article.text:
caleb.software
Goodbye Claude, Hello Pi
21 September 2026
#pi
#claude
I’ve been a longtime Claude Code user, ever since it became available in the Claude Pro subscription plan over a year ago. I remember the first time I used it, feeling giddy as it spat out messy Python code for whatever random weekend project I was working on, all from a single prompt. I’m certain that in a few years we’ll all look back at its release as one of the major drivers of this new era of software development we’re in.
Despite this, due to an accumulation of many small frustrations, I’ve finally decided to retire it as my main coding harness and migrate my development setup to use Pi instead.
Someone at Anthropic must’ve caught wind… just a day after making my decision, they announced Claude Code would finally start supporting AGENTS.md files in an effort to get me to stay. Unfortunately, for me it was too little, too late.
Complaining
In lieu of a proper obituary, I’d like to take this time to say a few words about the things I liked least about Claude Code (and thus what I’m looking forward to avoiding with Pi).
The AGENTS.md thing kind of epitomizes the whole reason I decided to quit using Claude Code. Don’t get me wrong, having a ton of CLAUDE.md files scattered about various GitHub hobby repos is great guerrilla marketing. But it sucks for users to have to deal with copying or symlinking between the two formats.
Like the Luddite I am, I still prefer to review most of the code it churns out before I commit it. I use(d) Claude Code inside VSCode, and it lets you connect the harness to the IDE. This is nice because you can highlight text in a file and have it automatically included in the context when asking questions or requesting changes during a review.
Except you can only have one session “connected” to the IDE at a time. If you open a second tab to start another task while the first one works, it can’t receive the text selection events from the IDE at all. This has been reported at least as far back as December 2025… and closed as a duplicate of a totally unrelated bug.1
Of course, you can always use the official Claude Code VSCode GUI extension, which does allow you to have multiple tabs open and load the text selection into the context of each. But this extension has plenty of problems of its own. Half of the built-in slash commands don’t work at all in the GUI. It doesn’t have any support for a custom status line. Subagent output messages are simply layered into the main chat thread in chronological order, which is a mess to read when more than one is running. I could go on and on.
In spite of all of these existing issues, it seems like Anthropic has worked at a feverish pace to pack more features into Claude Code without much care for quality or stability. Dynamic workflows, agent teams, ultrareviews – all great ways to help enterprise customers burn ever more tokens each day, but not really anything I want or need.
Alongside all of these feature releases, they always seem to be fiddling with things in ways that mess up my personal setup. At the time of writing, there have been 244 releases to Claude Code this year; over 3/4 of these changed the system prompt or tool descriptions, which can substantially change how the LLM performs (especially when these new instructions contradict user prompts or repo conventions).
And what are all those changes for? Despite chopping 80% of the system prompt, Claude Code still has way more overhead than Pi for seemingly no benefit. The default Bash tool’s description is almost 3,000 tokens, most of which is random stuff about using git and opening PRs on GitHub.2 The models already know how to do this without detailed instructions, by the way.3
Looking Forward
This post has been a lot of hating. I’m sorry! That’s not my usual style, and I do think Anthropic has made a really cool piece of software here. I’m also not under any delusion that I would’ve done a better job if I were the one in charge of…

comments.author: lukebuehler
comments.text:
People are giving all kinds of explanations here why Goldman is doing this, but they are not addressing what the article (implicitly) says: operating coding agents on the primary machines of finance professionals runs directly into the lethal trifecta. It's as simple as that.
You cannot have semi-unattended agents running on the same workstations that have access to client/trade/prop information and email client, and internet, and internal networks, it's too dangerous--a major leak is just one…

comments.author: legitster
comments.text:
At our org they have been clawing back Claude access because of chronic billing overages. Budgets are tight and consumption billing models are being stamped down on everywhere. Anthropic sales can not offer us any sort of normalized billing rate.
Gemini is swooping in because they offer flat consistent billing and handle overages through throttling access to higher models. For 90% of the non-engineering org the experience is near enough it makes no difference.

article.title: Goldman Sachs Is Pulling Claude Code From Its Bankers and Traders | State of AI
article.text:
Image Credit: State of AI
AI & Technology
Goldman Sachs Is Pulling Claude Code From Its Bankers and Traders
In July, Goldman's tech chief was praising the tools traders built with AI coding agents. New internal guidance hands those agents back to the engineers, weeks before Goldman takes Anthropic public.
ByState of AI Editorial
Nov 2, 2026
Goldman Sachs has restricted Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to its engineers, cutting off traders and bankers who used the tools to track client flows and build market models. The bank barred its Hong Kong bankers from Claude in April and is now a lead underwriter on Anthropic's IPO.
Most traders and bankers at Goldman Sachs can no longer use AI coding tools at work. Internal guidance updated in October restricts Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to the bank's engineers, Bloomberg News reported, following a review of productivity and risk concerns.
Strats, who work across trading, quantitative research and software engineering, still have access, according to a second person familiar with the matter.
The change has frustrated some traders, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. They had been using the tools to monitor client trading flows, model market moves and positions, and put together written and graphic material. Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra said the bank makes certain AI tools available to staff "to determine the best use cases" across the firm.
Argenti was praising trader-built tools in July
As recently as July, chief information officer Marco Argenti was talking up "vibe coding" by Goldman's non-technical employees. He told Bloomberg that traders and bankers had built tools with AI and passed them to the firm's engineers, of whom there are about 12,000, to be improved.
That arrangement let the people closest to a problem build a first version without waiting for engineering time. It also meant thousands of employees without engineering training were running software that writes and executes code, on the same machines they use to handle client information.
At a conference in Turin last month, Argenti described Goldman's AI adoption in waves and said developers, more than 12,000 of the bank's roughly 47,000 staff, had made up the first. The October guidance limits the coding agents to that group.
Goldman restricted Claude in Hong Kong in April
In April, Goldman removed Claude from its internal AI platform for bankers in Hong Kong. The Financial Times reported that the bank had read its contract with Anthropic strictly, and an Anthropic spokesperson said Claude had never been officially supported in Hong Kong. ChatGPT and Gemini remained available there. JPMorgan removed Claude from its Hong Kong approved list in June.
The Hong Kong restriction was based on location and contract terms, and the new one is based on role. Goldman's in-house AI assistant, which uses models from several companies, is still available across the firm. The restriction applies to third-party agents that can write and run code by themselves.
Goldman is still working closely with Anthropic
Earlier this year, Goldman said Anthropic engineers had spent six months at the bank helping build Claude-based agents for trade accounting and client onboarding. Those agents sit in the back office and are run by Goldman's engineering teams.
Goldman and Morgan Stanley are also the lead underwriters on Anthropic's IPO, according to the S-1 filed October 26. Anthropic is expected to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT before the end of November, as we reported last week. Over the next few weeks, Goldman's bankers will be marketing shares in a company whose coding agent most of them are no longer allowed to use.
Why a coding agent is riskier on a trading desk
Claude Code reads files, writes programs and runs them, typically with the same access as the person using it. Code an engineer writes with it usually goes through review, testing and deployment controls before it reaches…

article.title: Voice Chat with Agents · Cursor
article.text:
Nov 6, 2026 · Changelog
Changelog
Voice Chat with Agents
You can now talk with your agents in a realtime voice call. Describe a change out loud, ask what an agent is working on, and hear updates as the work moves forward.
Voice chat works in the Agents Window, the IDE, on web, and in Cursor for iOS.
#Start a call
When the agent is idle and the chat input is empty, click the waveform button labeled Start voice chat. It sits where Send usually is, next to the microphone button for dictation.
On iOS, you can also say "Hey Siri, call Cursor" to start a call with a new agent, and mute or hang up from the Lock Screen with a Live Activity.
#Talk while the agent works
The voice agent listens, replies, and hands coding work to the agent in your chat. While that agent runs, you can keep the conversation going. Ask what changed in a diff, check on a run, search earlier messages and calls with this agent, or switch between workers in a Project that has them.
The coding agent speaks for itself too. It shares short progress notes while it works and a brief answer when it's done, so you usually hear a short update instead of the full written reply.
#Powered by Grok Voice
Voice chat runs on Grok Voice. Pick from many voices in Voice settings, including Ara, Eve, Leo, Rex, and Sal. With Privacy Mode on, voice chat runs with zero data retention.
#Voice chat and dictation
Voice chat is separate from dictation, which earlier releases called Voice Mode. Dictation still turns your speech into text in the chat input, and Cmd+Shift+Space still toggles it in the IDE. Voice chat is a two-way conversation where the agent answers out loud.
Update Cursor to try voice chat. Learn more in our docs.

article.title: The components of agent memory \ Anthropic
article.text:
The components of agent memory
Published
Nov 6, 2026
Team
Engineering
Topics
Agents
Context engineering
Agent memory
Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward, but it must be lived forward. We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents.
As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. The hippocampus plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only some experiences are consolidated into long-term knowledge.
Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet rest, the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill those experiences and integrate them into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge.
Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed sleep-time compute as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often called dreaming (Figure 1).
We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization.
Claude can use dreaming to organize memory. This can correct mistakes, create notes, build new memory representations, or shape what’s preemptively loaded into future sessions.
Memory notes
By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), in-context learning (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and compaction (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window).
In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can mark a memory as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay, helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory.
Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can write them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next?
Claude can write notes to memory.
Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need
Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions.
Consider a task from Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0, a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.
Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it…

article.title: OpenAI Just Raised $11 Billion at a $1.25 Trillion Valuation, Below the $1.4 Trillion It First Sought - 24/7 Wall St.
article.text:
Investing
OpenAI Just Raised $11 Billion at a $1.25 Trillion Valuation, Below the $1.4 Trillion It First Sought
OpenAI got its money, but not on the terms it wanted, and the gap between its growth story and investor appetite is landing on two giants. One faces a bookkeeping hit, the other a deeper dependency on the funding flow.
By Omor Ibne Ehsan
Published November 7, 2026, 8:38am ET · 3 min read
𝕏
f
© 24/7 Wall St.
About $11 billion in new money reached OpenAI’s accounts by Friday, November 6, 2026, people familiar with the deal said. That cash is the first part of a round priced at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation, a figure the company’s CFO, Sarah Friar, confirmed in a TV interview. OpenAI declined to comment on the funding.
Press reports said OpenAI first set out to raise $30 billion or more at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Two investors put the first ask at $1.5 trillion. Friar challenged that account on air, saying the higher figure started with a media report and never came from OpenAI.
Whichever starting point you accept. The round ended up smaller and cheaper after AI stocks sold off, even as OpenAI says its business is accelerating. That gap affects shareholders of Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction) and NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) because both depend on OpenAI’s ability to fund its plans.
Cash Wired Versus Cash Promised
The closed amount covers about 37% of the original target. SoftBank and Abu Dhabi’s MGX took part in the round.
The rest could lift the total to as much as $20 billion, and a separate report put the follow-on at up to another $9 billion. That second portion has not closed. Lead investors, terms, and use of proceeds were not disclosed.
Friar called the price almost 50% above March, when OpenAI raised $122 billion at $852 billion. The implied step-up is roughly 46.7%, but treat it as approximate, because her figure is pre-money and March’s basis is unclear.
Growth Claims Meet a Tighter Market
Friar said OpenAI’s business grew 70% quarter over quarter in the third quarter, its enterprise business doubled, and revenue splits about 50% each between consumer and enterprise. She cited 1.2 billion weekly ChatGPT users and an ads run rate of $1 billion by August.
She gave no revenue dollar figures. Asked about the election, she said, “The demand for AI is real.”
Investors still paid less than the earliest reported asking price. Rival Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq in mid-November. Some investors now value it at about $1.5 trillion, down from roughly $2 trillion in earlier expectations.
Microsoft Feels This Through GAAP Earnings
Microsoft closed at $530.61, down 0.99%, for a market value of $3.94 trillion. The funding report came out around the close, so that move had other causes.
Gains on the OpenAI stake added $207 million to GAAP net income in the September quarter, compared with $3.1 billion in net losses a year earlier. A smaller valuation increase reduces future gains on the stake, although that is minor next to 48% Azure growth.
NVIDIA Depends on This Money Flowing
NVIDIA rose 2.78% to $186.64 as chip stocks rallied, and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) added 0.78%. NVIDIA is still down 21.4% over one month.
NVIDIA has said OpenAI’s existing and planned commitments add up to about 12 gigawatts of its compute. Management also said frontier labs “are growing faster than what their balance sheets and credit profiles can support.” A round that fills in stages shows that strain.
What OpenAI’s Smaller Round Means for AI Stock Investors
The optimistic view is that demand still exceeds supply. Microsoft says it has more demand than capacity, and NVIDIA guided to $108.0 billion in third-quarter revenue.
The bearish argument depends on financing. Private valuations can drop further, the second portion may close below full size, and a weak Anthropic debut could pull both labs’ valuations down.
